newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel first quarter tax revenues up 4.7 pct.
newsitem.headline: Israel first quarter tax revenues up 4.7 pct.

text.p: The Israeli government's revenues from taxes and fees in the first quarter totalled 26.8 billion shekels ($7.98 billion), up a real 4.7 percent from a year earlier, the Treasury announced on Thursday.
It added that discounting changes in tax regulations, the rise was only one percent.
Income and purchase taxes rose a real seven percent to 14.7 billion shekels in the quarter. Income tax revenue alone rose 10.6 percent but purchase tax revenue fell 28 percent.
Revenue from customs and value added tax amounted to 11.5 billion shekels, a rise of two percent.
Finance Minister Dan Meridor said on Thursday that the Treasury will decide in two weeks whether additional cuts in the 1997 budget are needed.
"In the next two weeks we will study the first quarter data and then decide," said Meridor, speaking at a seminar sponsored by Israel's diamond industry in Tel Aviv.
Meridor said revenue figures were most important as revenue had been lagging the Treasury's forecast because of a slowdown in economic growth.
Private sector economists said that first-quarter tax revenues were only about 250 million shekels below the forecast, which they estimated equalled a shortfall of 1.5 billion shekels for the year.
Israel in March posted a budget surplus of 188 million shekels, which was in line with the Treasury's target, officials said.
But the government had a deficit for the first quarter of 1.37 billion shekels. The Treasury declined to say how far above target the quarterly deficit was.
Bank of Israel Governor Jacob Frenkel has been pushing hard for the Treasury to make cuts immediately to keep the deficit within the budgetary target of 2.8 percent of gross domestic product (GDP).
Pessimists among analysts say the government will miss that target by 0.8 percent of GDP, or three to four billion shekels.
The 197 billion shekel budget in 1997 already includes seven billion shekels in spending cuts.
